name: One Pro
tagline: A compact flagship that does almost everything right.
summary: Aster's 6.3-inch flagship pairs a sharp 5× periscope with the steadiest sustained performance we've measured this year and a seven-year update promise. Charging is slow and storage upgrades are steep, but few phones will age as gracefully.
pros: Holds peak performance through long gaming sessions with minimal throttling
5× periscope stays sharp indoors, where most rivals fall back to digital crops
Seven years of OS and security updates, committed in writing
3,000-nit panel stays readable in direct midday sun
Titanium frame keeps the weight under 200 g
cons: 40 W wired charging is slow next to ₹70,000 rivals
No charger in the box
Storage upgrades cost ₹20,000 per tier

reviews.summary: The most consistent camera system of 2026 and a chip that barely throttles; the only real compromise is charging speed.
Led our sustained-performance chart, finishing the 20-minute stress loop at 91% of its peak score.
Brilliant in the hand and built to last, but at this price we expected faster charging and a charger in the box.

highlights: Camera is consistent in every light

name: One
tagline: Most of the Pro, in a lighter and simpler package.
summary: The standard One shares the Pro's chip and update promise but drops the periscope camera and the titanium frame. At 170 g it is one of the lightest phones we've tested, and it finally gets a 120 Hz display.
pros: Same Aster Fusion 3 chip as the Pro, with one fewer GPU core
Very light at 170 g and easy to use one-handed
Seven years of updates keep the long-term cost low
120 Hz display arrives on the non-Pro model for the first time
cons: No telephoto — 2× is a sensor crop and softens quickly beyond that
4,000 mAh battery needs a top-up on heavy days
Base 128 GB storage fills fast with 4K video

reviews.summary: The sensible Aster: nearly all of the Pro's speed and software for ₹45,000 less.
The main camera is excellent; the missing telephoto is the one thing you will notice every week.

highlights: Battery is tight for heavy users

name: X5
tagline: Flagship speed and a 6,000 mAh battery at a mid-flagship price.
summary: Kairo's X5 combines the fastest Nexis chip, a 6,000 mAh silicon-carbon battery and 100 W charging for well under the price of the big flagships. Its 3× periscope is a real step up from last year, though software support trails Aster.
pros: Two-day battery for moderate users from the 6,000 mAh silicon-carbon cell
100 W wired charging goes from 1% to full in about 30 minutes
Fastest Nexis 9 Gen 5 chip at a lower price than most rivals
IP68 and IP69 ratings survive jets of hot water, not just dunks
Bright 4,500-nit LTPO panel
cons: Five years of updates — two fewer than Aster
Pre-installed apps on first boot need cleaning up
213 g is heavy for long one-handed use

reviews.summary: Top-three CPU and GPU scores and the longest battery rundown in our flagship group.
The camera finally matches the hardware; 3× portraits are excellent, night video is still a step behind Aster.
The best-value flagship of the year, if you can live with a few pre-installed apps.

name: Neo 3
tagline: The mid-ranger to beat under ₹30,000.
summary: The Neo 3 gets the basics right — a bright 120 Hz AMOLED, a 5,500 mAh battery and 80 W charging — and adds a Nexis 7 Gen 4 chip that handles games comfortably. Cameras are good in daylight but only average at night.
pros: 5,500 mAh battery routinely ends the day above 40%
80 W charging tops up from 20% to 80% in about 20 minutes
Bright 2,400-nit AMOLED with accurate colours in Natural mode
Four years of OS updates is generous at this price
cons: Night photos are noisy and soft at the edges
8 MP ultra-wide is noticeably weaker than the main camera
No wireless charging

reviews.summary: Our default recommendation under ₹30,000: fast, long-lasting and supported for four years.
Gaming performance is excellent for the price; just don't expect flagship night shots.

name: Edge 40
tagline: Curved-screen polish and wireless charging, now under ₹30,000.
summary: Tarsa's Edge 40 brings flagship touches to the mid-range: a 3× telephoto, wireless charging, IP68 and a curved 144 Hz pOLED. A recent price cut makes it a serious alternative to the Kairo Neo 3, though Tarsa's software is less refined.
pros: Real 3× telephoto — rare at this price
Wireless charging and IP68 at a mid-range price
Curved 144 Hz pOLED looks premium and is bright outdoors
50 MP front camera with autofocus is great for video calls
cons: Tarsa OS shows ads in some system apps until you disable them
Pulsar 8400 runs warm in long gaming sessions
Curved edges cause occasional accidental touches

reviews.summary: The telephoto and wireless charging make it feel like a phone from a class above.
Gorgeous hardware held back by software that needs a trip through settings to clean up.

name: 14 Pro
tagline: A 108 MP camera and a big battery at a budget-plus price.
summary: Novu's 14 Pro shares the Neo 3's Nexis 7 Gen 4 chip and 5,500 mAh battery for less money, trading down to a Full HD+ AMOLED, slower 45 W charging and a plastic build. A strong pick if battery and value matter most.
pros: Same Nexis 7 Gen 4 chip as phones costing ₹8,000 more
5,500 mAh battery comfortably lasts a day and a half
108 MP main camera produces detailed daylight shots
Clean 120 Hz AMOLED for the price
cons: Only three years of OS updates
45 W charging takes about an hour
IP54 is splash resistance only

reviews.summary: A lot of phone for ₹22,000 — the chip and battery are the highlights.
Daylight photos impress; the plastic build and short update promise hold it back.

tagline: Dependable basics for under ₹15,000.
summary: The Novu 14 covers the essentials — 5G, a 5,000 mAh battery and a 90 Hz screen — at an entry price. The HD+ LCD and modest chip make it best for calls, messaging and light apps rather than gaming.
pros: 5G and a 5,000 mAh battery at an entry-level price
Battery easily lasts a full day of light use
Clean software with few pre-installed apps
Keeps the headphone jack and microSD slot
cons: HD+ LCD looks soft next to AMOLED rivals
Nexis 6 Gen 3 stutters in heavier games
Only two years of OS updates

reviews.summary: A sensible first smartphone or backup phone; stretch your budget a little if you can.
The battery and 5G are the story; performance is strictly for everyday apps.

name: Book Pro 14
tagline: A Mini-LED pro laptop that lasts all day, even under load.
summary: The Book Pro 14 pairs Aster's M5 Pro chip with a superb 120 Hz Mini-LED display and an 18-hour tested battery. It is the best laptop we have tested for photo and video work, but RAM and storage are soldered and upgrades are expensive at purchase.

specs.ports: 3× USB-C (Thunderbolt-class), HDMI 2.1, SD card, magnetic charging, 3.5 mm

pros: Best-in-class Mini-LED display with 1,600-nit HDR highlights and near-perfect colour
Same performance on battery as when plugged in
18 hours in our web-browsing rundown
HDMI and an SD card slot save on dongles
Silent under light loads; the fans are rarely audible
cons: RAM and SSD are soldered — buy the spec you need on day one
Storage upgrades at purchase are expensive
1.55 kg is heavy for a 14-inch laptop

reviews.summary: The benchmark for creative laptops: fast, quiet and with a display nothing else matches.
Sustained multi-core output dropped just 4% across a 30-minute render loop.
A brilliant machine, priced like one. Students should look at the Air.

name: Book Air 13
tagline: The best all-round laptop for most people.
summary: Thin, silent and fanless, the Book Air 13 delivers 16 hours of real-world battery and enough M5 performance for coding, study and light photo editing. Two ports and a 60 Hz screen are the main trade-offs.
pros: Fanless and completely silent
16 hours in our battery rundown — two full lecture days
Excellent keyboard and one of the best trackpads we've tested
Weighs just 1.24 kg
16 GB of RAM is now standard
cons: Only two USB-C ports, both on the left side
60 Hz display looks less fluid than rivals
Throttles during long video exports

reviews.summary: The laptop we'd recommend to almost anyone, especially after the post-festive price cut.
Performance is more than enough for students; heavy video editors should step up to the Pro.

name: Slate 14
tagline: A featherweight OLED ultrabook with ports to spare.
summary: Veyra's Slate 14 is a 1.18 kg ultrabook with a 2.8K 120 Hz OLED, 32 GB of RAM and a full port selection including HDMI 2.1 and USB-A. Battery life is strong for an OLED machine and the haptic trackpad is excellent.
pros: 2.8K 120 Hz OLED with full DCI-P3 coverage
Very light at 1.18 kg
USB4, USB-A and HDMI 2.1 — no dongles needed
32 GB of RAM as standard
Precise haptic trackpad
cons: Glossy OLED reflects overhead lights
Fans become audible under sustained loads
Webcam is only 1080p

reviews.summary: The best Meridian OS ultrabook of the year, now at a much better price.
Fifteen hours of battery from an OLED machine is a genuine achievement.

name: Slate 16 Studio
tagline: A 4K OLED workstation for colour-critical work.
summary: The Slate 16 Studio is built for photo and video professionals: a factory-calibrated 4K OLED, a Strata G6 GPU, 2 TB of storage and an SD Express reader. It is heavy and battery life is middling, but RAM and storage are user-upgradeable.

specs.ports: 2× USB-C (Thunderbolt-class), 2× USB-A, HDMI 2.1, SD Express, 3.5 mm

pros: Factory-calibrated 4K OLED with an average ΔE under 1
User-upgradeable RAM and two SSD slots
SD Express reader and two Thunderbolt-class ports
Strata G6 GPU speeds up video exports
cons: 11 hours of battery — about 7 hours less than the Book Pro 14
1.95 kg and a 140 W charger make it a desk machine
Gets loud during long exports

reviews.summary: Out-of-the-box colour accuracy is the best we have measured on a Meridian OS laptop.
A brilliant desk-bound workstation that is not designed for daily commuting.

name: Strike 16
tagline: Uncompromising gaming performance — with the weight to match.
summary: Corvex's flagship gaming laptop combines a Helix H9 HX chip with a Strata G8 running at its full 175 W limit and a 240 Hz Mini-LED. It tops our gaming charts, but it is heavy, loud under load and short on battery. Rising memory costs have nudged its price up this month.
pros: Fastest laptop GPU performance we have tested
240 Hz Mini-LED with excellent HDR highlights
User-upgradeable RAM and two SSD slots
Full port selection, including 2.5 GbE
cons: 2.6 kg plus a large 330 W power brick
About six hours of battery in light use
Fans exceed 50 dB in performance mode

reviews.summary: Top of our gaming leaderboard, with sustained clocks thanks to a vapour-chamber cooler.
A desktop replacement in every sense, including the noise and the weight.

name: Strike 15
tagline: Proper gaming performance without the flagship price.
summary: The Strike 15 pairs a Helix H7 HX processor with a Strata G6 GPU and a 165 Hz display at a mid-range price — even more so after its festive price cut. The Full HD screen is dim and battery life is short, but upgrades are easy.

specs.ports: USB-C, 3× USB-A, HDMI 2.1, Gigabit Ethernet, 3.5 mm

pros: Strata G6 runs most games at high settings in 1080p
Post-festive price cut makes it excellent value
Two SODIMM slots and a spare SSD slot are easy to reach
Good port selection, including Ethernet
cons: Dim 300-nit panel with limited colour range
About 6.5 hours of battery
Plastic lid flexes under pressure

reviews.summary: The gaming laptop most people should buy, especially at the current price.
Strong frame rates; the display is the clear corner that was cut.

name: Book 15
tagline: An honest, upgradeable laptop for first-year students.
summary: The Tarsa Book 15 doesn't chase specs: it offers 16 GB of RAM, a 512 GB SSD, a comfortable full-size keyboard and 10 hours of battery at a budget price. The screen is the weak point.
pros: 16 GB of RAM and a 512 GB SSD at a budget price
Comfortable keyboard with a number pad
Easy to upgrade RAM and storage later
10 hours of battery in our web test
cons: Washed-out display covers only 45% of DCI-P3
Plastic chassis creaks slightly
Speakers are thin and quiet

reviews.summary: The laptop we'd buy for a first-year student on a tight budget.
Everyday performance is fine; avoid it for photo editing.

name: C2 65
tagline: The best TV picture we've measured this year, in a 65-inch size.
summary: Lumora's C2 OLED pairs perfect blacks with a brighter 2026 panel, four HDMI 2.1 ports and a 144 Hz mode for PC gaming. It is our top pick for dark-room movie nights, and it is cheaper after the festive sales.
pros: Perfect blacks and pixel-level contrast
1,500-nit highlights — 50% brighter than last year's C1
Four full-bandwidth HDMI 2.1 ports with 144 Hz support
Dolby Vision, HDR10 and an accurate filmmaker mode
Fast Vista OS with a lighter home screen
cons: Not as bright as Mini-LED sets in sunlit rooms
Speakers lack deep bass — budget for a soundbar
Wide stand needs a large TV unit

reviews.summary: Contrast, colour accuracy and motion handling are all class-leading.
The best TV for movie nights this year, and finally bright enough for daytime cricket.
Input lag of 9.6 ms at 4K 120 Hz is among the lowest we have recorded.

name: C2 55
tagline: Flagship OLED picture quality at a more manageable size.
summary: The 55-inch C2 delivers the same panel technology, processing and four HDMI 2.1 ports as the 65-inch, making it the sweet spot of Lumora's range for most Indian living rooms.
pros: Same perfect blacks and processing as the 65-inch
Four HDMI 2.1 ports with 144 Hz support
Excellent near-black detail for movie watching
Slim 45 mm panel looks great wall-mounted
cons: Brightness dips on large, bright scenes (auto-dimming)
Thin built-in sound
No HDR10+ support

reviews.summary: The best-value way into flagship OLED performance.
If your room is under 12 feet across, this is the C2 to buy.

name: C1 55
tagline: Last year's OLED, now replaced by the C2.
summary: The 2025 C1 was our top OLED pick last year. It has been replaced by the brighter C2 and is archived; remaining stock is limited.
pros: Perfect blacks and wide viewing angles
Four HDMI 2.1 ports
Often discounted while stock lasts
cons: 1,000-nit peak is dimmer than the C2
Older Vista OS build feels slower
Limited availability

reviews.summary: An outstanding OLED that set the bar for 2025.
Superb in a dark room; the C2 improves brightness noticeably.

name: Vision Q8 65
tagline: Mini-LED brightness for bright living rooms.
summary: Kairo's Q8 brings 2,500-nit Mini-LED brightness, more than a thousand dimming zones and Dolby Vision to a 65-inch screen for far less than an OLED. Blooming is visible in dark scenes, but it shines — literally — in sunlit rooms.
pros: 2,500-nit highlights cut through daylight glare
Supports both Dolby Vision and HDR10+
144 Hz with VRR for consoles and PCs
Capable 60 W speakers with a built-in subwoofer
cons: Visible blooming around subtitles in dark scenes
Only two HDMI 2.1 ports
Narrow viewing angles

reviews.summary: Exceptional brightness for the money; contrast trails OLED in dark rooms.
Our pick for living rooms with big windows, especially at the new price.

name: Vision Q6 55
tagline: A well-rounded 4K QLED for the price of a budget set.
summary: The Q6 is a solid mid-range 55-inch TV with Dolby Vision, 120 Hz and VRR. It cannot match Mini-LED contrast, but colours are vivid and StreamOS is quick.
pros: 120 Hz with VRR — rare at this price
Dolby Vision and HDR10+ support
Quick StreamOS with all major Indian streaming apps
Accurate filmmaker preset out of the box
cons: Edge-lit panel looks greyish in dark scenes
600-nit peak limits HDR impact
Feet are not height-adjustable

reviews.summary: The best-value 120 Hz TV for current-generation consoles.
Good colour, limited contrast. A solid all-rounder.

name: Frame 50
tagline: A no-fuss 4K TV for everyday streaming.
summary: The Frame 50 is a simple 4K LED TV with StreamOS, HDR10 and a 60 Hz panel. Picture quality is fine in daytime but limited in contrast, and its price has ticked up slightly as panel costs rise.
pros: 4K streaming with a fast, ad-light StreamOS build
Slim bezels look more expensive than the price suggests
Three HDMI ports and optical out for a soundbar
cons: 60 Hz only, with no VRR
Low 350-nit peak limits HDR
No Dolby Atmos

reviews.summary: Fine for daily streaming; don't buy it for HDR movies or gaming.
Simple and reliable, with an interface that's quicker than most budget sets.

name: Frame 43
tagline: A compact Full HD smart TV for bedrooms and small rooms.
summary: The Frame 43 is a basic Full HD smart TV running StreamOS. It is the most affordable set in our rankings and best suited to bedrooms, kitchens or as a second TV.
pros: Low price for a reliable smart TV
StreamOS includes every major streaming app
Light enough to wall-mount without help
cons: Full HD resolution looks soft from up close
Weak contrast and narrow viewing angles
Only two HDMI ports

reviews.summary: A sensible second TV; look elsewhere for a main living-room set.
Basic picture, good software, low price.

name: Aura Max
tagline: The quietest, most comfortable headphones we've tested.
summary: Halden's Aura Max combines 42 dB of measured noise cancellation with a warm, detailed sound and memory-foam cushions that stay comfortable for an entire flight. They are expensive at full price, but frequently discounted.
pros: Best noise cancellation we have measured — 42 dB average attenuation
Comfortable for six-hour sessions
32 hours of battery with ANC on
Eight microphones keep calls clear on busy streets
LE Audio and multipoint for two devices
cons: Does not fold flat — the case is bulky
No water resistance
Expensive at full price

reviews.summary: Class-leading ANC without the pressure sensation; the sound is warm but detailed.
Our new pick for commutes and flights.
Superb, but the bulky case is a real annoyance in a backpack.

name: Pods Pro 3
tagline: Excellent earbuds, especially inside the Aster ecosystem.
summary: The Pods Pro 3 offer strong noise cancellation, a secure fit and the best call quality of any earbuds we've tested. Seamless switching and spatial audio work best with Aster devices.
pros: Best call quality of any earbuds we've tested
Strong ANC with a natural-sounding transparency mode
Secure, comfortable fit with four tip sizes
IP57 rating shrugs off sweat and rain
cons: Automatic device switching works only between Aster devices
No high-resolution codec support
Eight hours per charge trails the Kairo Buds 4 Pro

reviews.summary: An exceptionally natural transparency mode and very good ANC.
The obvious pick for Aster phone owners; less compelling otherwise.

name: Studio 2
tagline: Reference-grade wired sound for focused listening.
summary: The Studio 2 is an open-back wired headphone with a wide soundstage, superb detail and velour pads. It has no noise cancellation, battery or Bluetooth — which our weighted score penalises — but for critical listening at a desk it is the best-sounding headphone here.
pros: The most detailed and natural sound in our rankings
Wide, open soundstage
Velour pads stay cool over long sessions
Replaceable cable, pads and headband
cons: Open-back design leaks sound and blocks no outside noise
Wired only — sounds best with a decent DAC or amplifier
No microphone, so not suitable for calls

reviews.summary: Exceptional tonal balance and imaging. Judge it on sound alone.
Ranks low on our weighted chart only because it skips wireless features entirely.

name: Buds 4 Pro
tagline: Flagship-level ANC and battery for under ₹10,000.
summary: Kairo's Buds 4 Pro deliver strong noise cancellation, a high-resolution codec and 36 hours of total battery for a fraction of flagship prices. Calls are good rather than great.
pros: 40 dB measured ANC — close to flagship earbuds
36 hours of total battery with the case
Hi-Res 24-bit codec and LE Audio support
Multipoint works with any phone
cons: Calls sound processed in windy conditions
Bass-heavy default tuning (the EQ fixes it)
Glossy case scratches easily

reviews.summary: Remarkable ANC for the money; tune the EQ and they sound excellent.
The earbuds we'd buy under ₹10,000.

name: Buds Pro 2
tagline: Real noise cancellation at a budget price.
summary: Novu's Buds Pro 2 bring respectable ANC, multipoint and 40 hours of total battery to the sub-₹4,000 segment. The sound is a little bass-heavy but enjoyable.
pros: Effective ANC for bus and metro rides
Multipoint pairing with two devices
40 hours of total battery life
Good companion app with a 10-band EQ
cons: Microphones struggle in traffic
Average fit for small ears
No wireless charging

reviews.summary: The best ANC under ₹4,000 by a clear margin.
Great value; call quality is the main compromise.

name: Buds Air 2
tagline: Reliable everyday earbuds for under ₹2,000.
summary: The Buds Air 2 skip ANC but offer a comfortable fit, a stable connection and 42 hours of total battery. A small price rise this month still leaves them excellent value.
pros: 42 hours of total battery
Light, comfortable fit for long wear
Low-latency game mode
IPX4 sweat resistance
cons: No active noise cancellation
Thin bass at higher volumes
No multipoint

reviews.summary: Basic, comfortable and dependable — exactly what they promise.
Fine for podcasts and calls; music lovers should spend a bit more.

name: Siege 7
tagline: A comfortable wireless gaming headset with a 60-hour battery.
summary: The Siege 7 connects over a low-latency 2.4 GHz dongle and Bluetooth at the same time, lasts 60 hours and has one of the clearest boom mics we've tested. There's no noise cancellation, so it's best used at home.
pros: 60-hour battery
Clear detachable boom mic for team chat
Low-latency 2.4 GHz and Bluetooth at the same time
Light clamping force and breathable pads
cons: No active noise cancellation
Too bulky for commuting
Gaming EQ presets are bass-heavy

reviews.summary: Measured latency of 18 ms over 2.4 GHz — excellent for competitive play.
Comfortable and long-lasting; music playback is merely average.

name: Pad Pro 13
tagline: The most powerful tablet you can buy — priced accordingly.
summary: The Pad Pro 13 pairs the M5 chip with a tandem OLED display that's as good as any laptop screen. Stylus and keyboard support are excellent, but the accessories add significantly to the price.
pros: Tandem OLED with 1,600-nit HDR highlights
M5 chip handles 4K video editing with ease
Thin and light at 579 g for a 13-inch tablet
Four-speaker audio is the best on any tablet
cons: Stylus and keyboard cost extra — over ₹40,000 together
AsterOS still limits desktop-style multitasking
Expensive storage tiers

reviews.summary: The best tablet display and performance, by a distance.
The M5 led every tablet benchmark we ran.
Brilliant hardware, but most people don't need this much power.

name: Pad Air 11
tagline: The tablet sweet spot for students and creatives.
summary: The Pad Air 11 offers M4 performance, full stylus support and a laminated display at a much lower price than the Pro. It's our top pick for students who take notes and sketch.
pros: M4 performance for note-taking, sketching and light editing
Pro-grade stylus support with low latency
Laminated display with an anti-reflective coating
Excellent app ecosystem
cons: 60 Hz display — the stylus feels less fluid than on 120 Hz tablets
128 GB base storage
Stylus sold separately

reviews.summary: The tablet most students should buy, especially after the price cut.
Fast and polished; the 60 Hz screen is the one area that feels dated.

name: Pad 11
tagline: The simple, well-supported tablet for the whole family.
summary: The entry Pad 11 gets the Aster Fusion 3 chip and long software support at a mid-range price. It supports a first-generation stylus and a keyboard, making it a capable study tablet.
pros: Long software support from Aster
Fast enough for every everyday app and game
Supports stylus and keyboard accessories
Reliable 10-hour battery
cons: Non-laminated display shows a gap under the glass
Only 60 Hz
The basic stylus is sold separately

reviews.summary: Still the default family tablet, now with a faster chip.
Plenty fast; the Kairo Pad 3 has the better screen for less money.

name: Pad 3 Pro
tagline: A flagship chip and a 144 Hz display — coming soon to India.
summary: Kairo's upcoming Pad 3 Pro pairs the Nexis 9 Gen 5 with a 12.1-inch 144 Hz display and a 10,000 mAh battery. Our scores are provisional, based on early lab results, and will be verified at launch.
pros: Nexis 9 Gen 5 leads our early tablet benchmarks
Sharp 144 Hz 3K display
Large 10,000 mAh battery
Stylus and keyboard support
cons: Kairo's tablet app ecosystem is smaller
No cellular model planned for India
Final pricing not yet confirmed

reviews.summary: Early sample: excellent CPU and GPU results; software is still in beta.
Hands-on: the 144 Hz display is a highlight; we'll test battery life at launch.

name: Pad 3
tagline: A 144 Hz tablet for streaming and study at a mid-range price.
summary: The Pad 3 offers a sharp 2.8K 144 Hz display, quad speakers and a 13-hour battery for well under ₹30,000. Stylus support is good; app optimisation is the weak point.
pros: Sharp 2.8K 144 Hz display
13 hours of video playback
Four loud, clear speakers
Stylus and keyboard support
cons: Some apps aren't optimised for large screens
No cellular option
Stylus sold separately

reviews.summary: The best-value tablet for streaming and study — and now cheaper still.
A great screen for the money; app support is the trade-off.

name: Tab 11
tagline: A basic tablet for streaming, reading and kids.
summary: The Novu Tab 11 is an affordable 11-inch tablet with a 90 Hz screen and an LTE option. It's fine for streaming and reading, but 4 GB of RAM limits multitasking.
pros: Low price, with an LTE variant
11-inch 90 Hz screen is good for video
Ten hours of video playback
Expandable storage via microSD
cons: 4 GB of RAM struggles with multitasking
No stylus support
Slow 15 W charging

reviews.summary: A fine streaming slate for the price; not a study tool.
Good for kids and video; anything heavier feels slow.

name: Canvas 12
tagline: A note-taking tablet with the pen in the box.
summary: Tarsa's Canvas 12 ships with a low-latency stylus and a 12.4-inch AMOLED with an optional paper-feel matte finish, making it the best-value note-taking tablet we've tested. Software support is shorter than Aster's.
pros: Stylus included in the box
Beautiful 12.4-inch 120 Hz AMOLED
14 hours of battery in our video test
Excellent handwriting-to-text conversion
cons: Four years of updates, versus longer support from Aster
Keyboard cover sold separately
Pulsar 8400 is mid-range for heavy editing

reviews.summary: The best note-taking tablet for the money, thanks to the bundled pen.
A superb screen and pen; the software polish isn't quite at Aster's level.

name: Studio Display 32
tagline: A 6K Mini-LED display for Aster creators — first look.
summary: Aster's upcoming 32-inch 6K Mini-LED display adds 120 Hz and 1,600-nit HDR highlights. This listing stays in draft until we complete full calibration testing.
pros: 6K resolution gives razor-sharp text at 32 inches
Mini-LED backlight with 1,600-nit HDR highlights
Single-cable connection with 96 W charging
Premium aluminium stand with height adjustment
cons: Very expensive
Some features only work with Aster computers
Only one upstream port

reviews.summary: Pre-production unit: impressive uniformity; full calibration results to follow.
First look: stunning sharpness, at a price few will pay.

name: Glow 27
tagline: QD-OLED for gamers who also edit photos.
summary: The Glow 27 pairs a 240 Hz QD-OLED panel with near-instant response times and a wide colour gamut. It's our top gaming monitor and surprisingly good for photo editing too.
pros: 0.03 ms response — no visible motion blur
240 Hz with Adaptive Sync
99% DCI-P3 coverage and true blacks
90 W USB-C for single-cable laptop setups
cons: Burn-in risk with static desktop elements over the years
Colour fringing visible on fine text
Glossy coating reflects lamps

reviews.summary: Exceptional motion clarity and colour volume; the best OLED monitor we've tested.
The lowest input lag in our 2026 test group.

name: Line 27 4K
tagline: Accurate 4K for photo editing on a sensible budget.
summary: The Line 27 4K is a factory-calibrated IPS monitor with 95% DCI-P3 coverage and USB-C. It's sharp, accurate and ergonomic — ideal for photo work and coding — but limited to 60 Hz.
pros: Factory calibration report in the box (ΔE under 2)
Sharp 4K text at 27 inches
65 W USB-C over a single cable
Height, tilt and pivot adjustments
cons: 60 Hz is not for gaming
DisplayHDR 400 is HDR in name only
Average contrast in dark rooms

reviews.summary: Excellent accuracy for the price; ideal for photographers.
A great productivity monitor, especially after the festive price cut.

name: View 27
tagline: The ultimate single-cable desk hub.
summary: The View 27 is a 4K 120 Hz IPS monitor with 90 W USB-C, Ethernet, a KVM switch and four USB-A ports — one cable connects your laptop to everything. Picture quality is excellent for work.

specs.ports: USB-C (Thunderbolt-class, 90 W), HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, RJ45, 4× USB-A, KVM

pros: 90 W USB-C charges most laptops
Built-in KVM, Ethernet and USB hub
120 Hz 4K makes scrolling smooth
Fully adjustable stand
cons: Not bright enough for impactful HDR
Stand base takes up desk space
No built-in speakers

reviews.summary: The best USB-C hub monitor we've used — it replaced our docking station.
A very good IPS panel; 120 Hz is a welcome upgrade.

name: View 24
tagline: A dependable Full HD office monitor.
summary: The View 24 is a no-nonsense 24-inch office monitor with a height-adjustable stand and a 100 Hz IPS panel. It's an easy pick for home offices on a budget.

100 Hz makes scrolling smoother
Flicker-free backlight with a low blue-light mode
VESA mount support
cons: No USB-C
Full HD looks soft at close range
No speakers

reviews.summary: A sensible home-office monitor with a stand you'd normally pay more for.
Basic but well built.

name: Arc 34
tagline: An immersive ultrawide for games and editing timelines.
summary: The Arc 34 is a 34-inch curved VA ultrawide with 180 Hz, strong contrast and 65 W USB-C. It's excellent for racing games and video timelines, and much cheaper after the festive sales.

specs.ports: 2× HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, USB-C (65 W), USB hub

pros: Deep VA contrast for dark scenes
180 Hz on a 3440 × 1440 panel
65 W USB-C and a USB hub
1500R curve feels immersive without distortion

Ultrawide support varies between games

reviews.summary: Very good contrast and smooth motion, with slight black smearing.
Great ultrawide value at its new price.

name: Pulse 25
tagline: A fast 240 Hz esports monitor at a budget price.
summary: The Pulse 25 is a 24.5-inch 240 Hz IPS esports monitor with a 1 ms response time and a fully adjustable stand. Colour and resolution are basic, but it's built for competitive gaming.
pros: 240 Hz with a 1 ms response time
Fully adjustable stand
Low input lag
Affordable for a true esports panel
cons: Full HD resolution
Washed-out colours
No USB-C

reviews.summary: Measured a 1.2 ms average response with minimal overshoot.
The most affordable 240 Hz monitor we'd recommend.
